blocks.text: Token tasks are a family of fine-tuning problems that assign a label to every individual token in a text, rather than one label for the entire input, a structurally different problem from the sequence classification tasks, sentiment, intent, topic, all covered earlier in this module.

This topic covers the general shape of token classification problems, the BIO labeling scheme most token tasks use, and the subword tokenization alignment challenge that is specific to this task family, before the following two topics cover named entity recognition and part-of-speech tagging as specific examples.
1. Sequence Classification vs Token Classification

blocks.alt: Sequence classification assigns one label per text while token classification assigns one label per token

blocks.text: Sequence classification, covered earlier in this module, produces a single label for an entire input, token classification instead produces a separate label for every individual token in the input, a fundamentally different output shape that needs its own data format and evaluation approach.
2. What a Labeled Token Sequence Looks Like

blocks.alt: Individual tokens like Apple, is, and hiring each receive their own label

blocks.text: In a token classification example, "Apple is hiring", each word gets its own label, Apple might be labeled as the beginning of an organization name while is and hiring get an outside label, meaning they are not part of any entity being tagged.
3. The Family of Token Classification Tasks

blocks.alt: Named entity recognition, part of speech tagging, and other token tasks like chunking and slot filling

blocks.text: Named entity recognition, covered in the next topic, and part-of-speech tagging, covered in the topic after that, are the two most common token classification tasks, but the same underlying approach also covers chunking, grouping tokens into meaningful phrases, and slot filling, extracting structured values in a conversational system, closely related to the entity extraction mentioned in the earlier Intent Classification topic.
4. The Subword Tokenization Alignment Challenge

blocks.alt: A word level label needs alignment after subword tokenization

blocks.text: Labels are naturally assigned at the word level, but the tokenizer, covered in an earlier module, often splits a single word into multiple subword tokens, training code needs to carefully align word-level labels down to the subword token level, typically labeling only the first subword of a word and marking the rest to be ignored during loss computation.

blocks.title: Subword alignment is a common source of subtle bugs
blocks.content: Getting this alignment wrong, for instance applying the same label to every subword piece instead of just the first, can silently degrade token classification training without producing an obvious error.

blocks.text: 5. The BIO Labeling Scheme

blocks.alt: B for Begin, I for Inside, and O for Outside form the BIO scheme

blocks.text: Most token classification tasks use a BIO scheme, B marking the beginning of a labeled span, I marking tokens inside a span that continues from a previous token, and O marking tokens outside any labeled span, this lets the scheme represent multi-token entities or phrases, not just single-token labels.

blocks.text: 6. Token-Level vs Entity-Level Evaluation

blocks.alt: Token level accuracy is compared against entity level F1

blocks.text: Evaluating token classification purely at the individual token level can look deceptively good since most tokens are simply outside any entity, entity-level F1, requiring an entire multi-token span to be correctly identified and labeled, is the more meaningful metric for judging whether the model actually gets full entities or phrases right.
7. Data Annotation for Token Tasks

blocks.alt: Token by token labeling is compared against span highlight annotation

blocks.text: Annotating token classification data is generally more labor intensive than sequence classification, since every token needs a label rather than the whole text needing just one, tooling that lets annotators highlight spans directly, rather than labeling token by token, significantly speeds up this process in practice.
8. Model Architecture Considerations

Token classification fine-tuning typically adds a classification head applied at every token position rather than just at a single pooled representation, a structural difference from the sequence-level classification head covered in the general Classification topic, though both build on the same underlying pretrained model.
9. Where Token Tasks Fit in a Larger Pipeline

Token classification output commonly feeds into downstream systems, extracted entities populating a structured record, part-of-speech tags supporting a grammar or parsing tool, this topic and the two following it cover the fine-tuning side, while what happens with the extracted labels afterward is application specific.
Worked Example

A team building a document processing tool needs to extract company names and locations from unstructured text. They label a dataset using the BIO scheme, tagging each token as the beginning or continuation of an organization or location span, or outside any span.

After an initial training run, token-level accuracy looks very high since most tokens are outside labels, but entity-level F1 reveals the model frequently mislabels the boundary of multi-word company names, prompting the team to review and clean up boundary annotation consistency in their training data, which meaningfully improves entity-level F1 on a follow up run.
Common Mistakes

items: Misaligning word-level labels with subword tokens, applying the same label across all subword pieces incorrectly
Evaluating only with token-level accuracy, which looks deceptively high due to the prevalence of outside labels
Underestimating how labor intensive full token-by-token annotation is compared to sequence-level labeling
Inconsistent span boundary annotation in training data, causing the model to learn unclear boundary behavior

blocks.text: Practice

Take a short sentence containing at least one multi-word entity, a company or place name, and manually label it using the BIO scheme, then identify which subwords a typical tokenizer might split your entity into and how you would align the BIO labels down to that subword level.
Key Takeaway

Token classification assigns a label to every individual token rather than one label per input, using a BIO scheme to represent multi-token spans, and requires careful subword tokenization alignment along with entity-level rather than token-level evaluation, forming the shared foundation that named entity recognition and part-of-speech tagging, covered in the next two topics, both build on.
